ARGUS: Hera's Onboard Watchman

ARGUS is autonomous image triage proposed for ESA's Hera mission: software that watches the camera feed onboard, learns the scene as images arrive, and decides which images deserve downlink. This page runs the complete algorithm live, strictly frame by frame, over 404 real Asteroid Framing Camera images. The orange overlay marks the pixels that surprise the detector at each frame.

About ARGUS

ARGUS (Hera's Onboard Watchman for Autonomous Image Triage) is an experiment proposed for ESA's Hera mission through the OSIP call "Autonomous Software Experiments on Hera". Deep-space missions photograph far more than the radio link can carry home, and the judgment of which image matters is made on the ground days later. ARGUS moves that judgment onboard: a lightweight unsupervised detector learns the scene as images arrive, alerts on significant change, and keeps the stored record current as the view drifts.

The name comes from Greek myth: Argus Panoptes was the all-seeing giant who kept watch for Hera, some of a hundred eyes always open. The Hera spacecraft is on the way to the Didymos binary asteroid system to examine the aftermath of NASA's DART impact.

This page is the complete detection algorithm implemented in JavaScript and run strictly frame by frame over the 404 real Asteroid Framing Camera images distributed with the ESA call package. Every score, alert, and keep decision is computed live in the browser, and the sliders adjust the same thresholds a flight controller would set through configuration parameters. At the default settings ARGUS keeps 9 of 404 frames (about 9 MB of 420 MB) with zero false alarms across roughly 350 routine frames.
